newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's parliament adopts natural resources law.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's parliament adopts natural resources law.

text.p: Serbia's parliament adopted new laws on Wednesday governing the use of natural resources by domestic and foreign companies.

"Concessions can be granted only if they help further development of resources, guarantee technological and technical integrity of resources, provide efficient management and are environmentally friendly," Serbian Construction Minister Branislav Ivkovic told the parliament.

The government will grant concessions for exploration and exploitation of mineral ores. Interested parties can build, maintain and use energy facilities, gas and oil pipelines, roads, railways, telecommunications, airports and other utilities.
All concessions will be granted and supervised by a special government agency for investment, Ivkovic said.

"Concessions will be granted via tenders and those will be published in an international tenders bulletin. The final decision on granting concessions will be made by the Serbian government," Ivkovic told reporters.
The minister expected the first concession to be granted within two months for an infrastructure project.
Ivkovic expected roads to first attract foreign investors.

"Roads offer to investors a quick return on their investment. We are also interested in offering railways, but those provide a slower return to investors and that is where we shall have to do our best to attract investors, both domestic and foreign," Ivkovic told Reuters.

The minister also said time was needed to find out whether the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the World Bank would be ready to finance such investments either through credit support or via equity investment.

"Participation of big investors means participation of big banks," he said, adding most interest has been shown by American, British, French and Greek investors. "This is a clear law providing sufficient guarantees to those who wish to invest in the region to repatriate profit," he added.
All concessioners will be granted an initial five-year tax-relief, but the size and terms of the tax-break and repatriation of profit will be determined by the contract.
Foreigners can opt for a simple concession deal, create joint ventures with local companies or enter a deal with the government on an investment- and profit-sharing basis.
But Ivkovic insisted Serbia was mainly interested in granting concessions on a build-operate-transfer (BOT) basis.

Concessions can be granted for facilities and equipment founded by the Republic of Serbia or by local self-administrations only if those are exploited inefficiently, Ivkovic said. The new law excludes renewal and development of forests, game breeding and hunting.
